arguments.content:
Cancer “survival rate” in the U.S. is usually reported as the 5‑year relative survival rate: the percentage of people alive five years after diagnosis compared with similar people without cancer. These rates vary widely by cancer type and stage at diagnosis, and they improve over time with earlier detection and better treatments—so they’re best viewed as broad, population-level estimates rather than predictions for an individual.

- Merkel cell carcinoma — ~3,000 cases/year (US)  
- Uveal (ocular) melanoma — ~3,500 cases/year (US)  
- Anal cancer — ~10,000 cases/year (US)  
- Male breast cancer — ~2,800 cases/year (US)  
- Osteosarcoma — ~1,000 cases/year (US)  

- Mesothelioma (pleural/peritoneal) (5-year survival ~12%)  
- Esophageal cancer (5-year survival ~21%)  
- Liver & intrahepatic bile duct cancer (5-year survival ~21%)  
- Lung & bronchus cancer (5-year survival ~26%)  
- Acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (5-year survival ~31%)
